lead: Noise enters a receiver with the signal, and each detector treats it differently. The figure of merit (FOM) puts that difference into one number: the output signal-to-noise ratio divided by the channel signal-to-noise ratio, for the same received power and the same noise. It lets you compare AM, DSB-SC, SSB and FM before building anything. AM with an envelope detector reaches at most 1/3; DSB-SC and SSB with coherent detection reach 1; FM reaches (3/2)β², because wider deviation makes the message stand further above the discriminator noise. Link budgets for broadcast, satellite and two-way radio start from these numbers.
prereq: You need: white noise and its power spectral density (see Noise sources, white noise and AWGN), and the AM and DSB-SC detectors (see AM demodulation: envelope and coherent detectors).

sections.h3: The receiver model and the figure of merit

blocks.text: Model the receiver as a band-pass filter of the transmission bandwidth, a detector, and a low-pass filter of the message bandwidth W. The channel adds white noise of two-sided power spectral density N<sub>0</sub>/2 W/Hz. After the band-pass filter the noise is narrowband and can be written n(t) = n<sub>c</sub>(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub> t − n<sub>s</sub>(t) sin 2πf<sub>c</sub> t. The in-phase part n<sub>c</sub>(t) and the quadrature part n<sub>s</sub>(t) are low-pass noises, each with power spectral density N<sub>0</sub> over the filter band, and each carries the same power as n(t).

Let P be the average received signal power in watts, carrier and sidebands together. The channel signal-to-noise ratio is the received power over the noise power in the message band, (S/N)<sub>c</sub> = P/(N<sub>0</sub> W): the SNR a plain baseband system would get with the same power. The output signal-to-noise ratio (S/N)<sub>o</sub> is the message power over the noise power after the detector and the low-pass filter. Then:

blocks.where: both ratios as powers, for the same P, N<sub>0</sub> and W; FOM above 1 means the scheme does better than plain baseband, below 1 worse.

blocks.text: Some books measure the FM input noise in the transmission bandwidth B<sub>T</sub> instead of W. Their input SNR is smaller by B<sub>T</sub>/W, so their FOM is larger by B<sub>T</sub>/W = 2(β + 1). Always check which bandwidth a quoted FOM uses.

AM with an envelope detector: the signal is A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub> t] cos 2πf<sub>c</sub> t, with total power P = (A<sub>c</sub>²/2)(1 + m²/2). With a carrier well above the noise, the envelope is about A<sub>c</sub> + A<sub>c</sub> m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub> t + n<sub>c</sub>(t). After the dc block the message is A<sub>c</sub> m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub> t, power A<sub>c</sub>²m²/2, and the noise is n<sub>c</sub>(t) over |f| ≤ W, power 2N<sub>0</sub>W. So (S/N)<sub>o</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>²m²/(4N<sub>0</sub>W), while (S/N)<sub>c</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>²(1 + m²/2)/(2N<sub>0</sub>W). Dividing:

blocks.where: m is the modulation index, 0 ≤ m ≤ 1; the largest value, at m = 1, is 1/3 (−4.77 dB).

blocks.text: The carrier takes power without carrying the message, and that is the whole loss. With a weak carrier the envelope detector also has its own threshold, which the coherent detector does not.

DSB-SC with coherent detection: the signal A<sub>c</sub> m(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub> t has power A<sub>c</sub>²P<sub>m</sub>/2, where P<sub>m</sub> is the message power. Multiplying by cos 2πf<sub>c</sub> t and low-pass filtering gives (A<sub>c</sub>/2)m(t) + (1/2)n<sub>c</sub>(t): signal power A<sub>c</sub>²P<sub>m</sub>/4 and noise power 2N<sub>0</sub>W/4. So (S/N)<sub>o</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>²P<sub>m</sub>/(2N<sub>0</sub>W) = P/(N<sub>0</sub>W), and FOM = 1. The coherent product rejects n<sub>s</sub>.
SSB with coherent detection: the receiver filter is only W wide, so half the noise enters, but the detected message power is also halved. The two halves cancel: FOM = 1, in half the bandwidth.

sections.h3: FM: the discriminator shapes the noise

blocks.text: With a strong carrier the noise mainly tilts the carrier phasor; the phase error is about n<sub>s</sub>(t)/A<sub>c</sub>. The discriminator outputs (1/2π) times the rate of change of phase, and differentiating multiplies each noise component at frequency f by f. So the output noise power spectral density is N<sub>0</sub>f²/A<sub>c</sub>² across the IF band: flat noise in, parabolic noise out. Only |f| ≤ W gets through the low-pass filter, so:
N<sub>o</sub> is the output noise power; the output signal is the frequency swing Δf cos 2πf<sub>m</sub> t, power Δf²/2.

So (S/N)o = (Δf²/2)/(2N0W³/3Ac²) = (3/2)β² × (Ac²/2)/(N0W) with fm = W, and (S/N)c = (Ac²/2)/(N0W). Dividing gives FOMFM = (3/2)β². At β = 5 this is 37.5, or 15.74 dB. Doubling β quadruples the FOM but roughly doubles the bandwidth: FM trades bandwidth for SNR. The result needs the carrier above the FM threshold (see Threshold and capture effects).

examples.question: An AM receiver with m = 0.5 and an FM receiver with β = 5 receive the same power with the same noise, giving a channel SNR of 20 dB in the message bandwidth W = 5 kHz. Find each FOM, each output SNR and each transmission bandwidth.
steps: FM is 25.28 dB better for six times the bandwidth (Figure 3.5.1).
examples.answer: AM: FOM 0.111 (−9.54 dB), output 10.46 dB, 10 kHz. FM: FOM 37.5 (15.74 dB), output 35.74 dB, 60 kHz.

examples.question: A receiver needs an output SNR of 40 dB for a W = 15 kHz message. The noise is N<sub>0</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. Find the received power needed with AM (m = 1), DSB-SC, SSB and FM (β = 5), and check that the FM carrier is above a 10 dB threshold in its Carson bandwidth.
steps: Noise in the message band: N<sub>0</sub>W = 4 × 10⁻²¹ × 15 000 = 6 × 10⁻¹⁷ W.
DSB-SC and SSB: P = 6 × 10⁻¹³ W = −92.2 dBm.

Threshold check: B<sub>T</sub> = 2(5 + 1) × 15 = 180 kHz; noise in B<sub>T</sub> = 4 × 10⁻²¹ × 180 000 = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ W; carrier-to-noise ratio = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴/7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ = 22.2 = 13.5 dB, above 10 dB, so the FM figure holds.
examples.answer: AM −87.4 dBm, DSB-SC and SSB −92.2 dBm, FM −108.0 dBm (20.5 dB less than AM); the FM carrier is 13.5 dB above the noise in 180 kHz, so it is above threshold.

traps: AM's FOM is at most 1/3, not 1. At m = 1, FOM = 1/3 (−4.77 dB); only coherent DSB-SC and SSB reach 1.
(3/2)β² is not free: the bandwidth is 2(β + 1)W, and the formula fails below the FM threshold.
Do not mix conventions. (3/2)β² uses input noise in W; with input noise in B<sub>T</sub> = 2(β + 1)W the same receiver has FOM = 3β²(β + 1).
In dB, add: (S/N)<sub>o</sub> (dB) = (S/N)<sub>c</sub> (dB) + 10 log FOM. Never add a ratio to a dB value.
The FM output noise rises as f² in power, a triangle in amplitude. It is the noise that rises, not the signal.

quiz.q: Define the figure of merit of a receiver.
quiz.a: FOM = (S/N)<sub>o</sub>/(S/N)<sub>c</sub>: output SNR over channel SNR, where (S/N)<sub>c</sub> = P/(N<sub>0</sub>W) is the received power over the noise in the message band, for the same P and N<sub>0</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is the AM figure of merit at most 1/3?
quiz.a: The carrier takes power but carries no message. With total power (A<sub>c</sub>²/2)(1 + m²/2), only the m²/2 part is message, giving FOM = m²/(2 + m²), which is 1/3 at m = 1.

quiz.q: An AM receiver has m = 0.8 and a channel SNR of 30 dB. Find its FOM in dB and its output SNR.
An FM receiver has β = 3 and a channel SNR of 15 dB. Find its FOM and output SNR in dB.
quiz.a: FOM = 1.5 × 9 = 13.5 = 11.30 dB. Output SNR = 15 + 11.30 = 26.30 dB, if the carrier is above threshold.

quiz.q: Why does the FM output noise power rise as f² after the discriminator?
quiz.a: The noise mostly moves the carrier phase, by about n<sub>s</sub>(t)/A<sub>c</sub>. The discriminator outputs the rate of change of phase, and differentiation multiplies each component at frequency f by f, so the power spectral density is multiplied by f².

quiz.q: Same received power and W: AM with m = 1 against FM with β = 2. Compare output SNR and bandwidth.
quiz.a: AM FOM = 1/3 (−4.77 dB); FM FOM = 1.5 × 4 = 6 (7.78 dB). FM is 7.78 + 4.77 = 12.55 dB better. AM uses 2W, FM 2(2 + 1)W = 6W, three times wider.

quiz.q: A book quotes the FM FOM as 3β²(β + 1). What input-noise bandwidth does it use?

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital links keep the same bookkeeping under other names: noise figure, bandwidth and the Eb/N0 a modem needs. Analog FM survives in broadcasting and simple two-way radio, while most mobile voice moved to digital modulation and coding, which do better at low SNR. Search for FM improvement factor and threshold extension.

figure.caption: Output SNR against channel SNR for the three cases of worked example 1. Each line sits above or below the 0 dB line of DSB-SC and SSB by its figure of merit; at 20 dB in, AM gives 10.46 dB and FM 35.74 dB. The FM line is dashed below its threshold.
